edits.title: Docker namespaces and their purposes
bullets: Linux namespaces partition kernel resources, giving each container its own isolated view; Docker uses them to achieve process and resource isolation.
PID namespace isolates process IDs, giving each container independent process numbering.
UTS namespace provides separate hostname and domain name for each container.
MNT namespace gives each container its own mount point hierarchy.
IPC namespace isolates inter‑process communication resources such as shared memory and semaphores.
NET namespace gives each container its own network stack, interfaces, and IP addresses.
addresses_questions: What are the main types of namespaces Docker uses?
What is a Linux namespace and why does Docker use them?

edits.title: Docker Improves Application Portability
bullets: Docker is an open‑platform tool that packages an app, its runtime, libraries, and settings into an immutable image.
Docker solves the “works on my machine” problem by ensuring the same image runs unchanged on any host with a compatible Docker engine.
Because Docker images contain only user‑space components, they share the host kernel, avoiding the overhead of a full guest OS used by VMs.
Containers differ from VMs: VMs virtualize hardware and run separate guest OSes; containers virtualize at the OS level and share the host kernel.
The shared‑kernel model makes containers lightweight virtualization, requiring fewer resources and starting in seconds.
Main Docker benefits: portability across environments, fast provisioning, consistent runtime, dependency isolation, and simplified CI/CD workflows.

edits.title: Containers share host OS kernel
bullets: Containers run as isolated user‑space processes but share the host operating system’s kernel.
They share the kernel’s system calls, device drivers, and kernel-level resources, while each container has its own filesystem and libraries.
This shared kernel model provides lightweight isolation and fast startup compared to full virtual machines.

edits.title: Namespace creation and joining details
bullets: Before unshare, a process shares its parent’s namespaces; after unshare, the specified namespaces are created anew for the calling process (PID takes effect after a subsequent fork).
setns(fd) attaches the calling process to the namespace referred to by the file descriptor, moving it into an existing namespace hierarchy.
clone(CLONE_NEWNS|SIGCHLD) creates a child with a new mount namespace that initially contains the parent’s mounts.
The new mount namespace initially mirrors the parent’s mounts; later mounts or unmounts affect only the child.
UTS namespaces can be nested; a hostname change inside a child UTS namespace is invisible to the parent and any sibling namespaces.
A diagram on the slide shows the hierarchy before and after unshare, with separate branches for the new namespaces.

edits.title: Veth pair creation and chroot vs pivot_root comparison
bullets: Create a veth pair: ip link add veth0 type veth peer name veth1
Move ends into namespaces: ip link set veth0 netns <ns1>; ip link set veth1 netns <ns2>
Inside each namespace, bring the interface up and assign unique IPs (e.g., veth0 10.0.0.1/24, veth1 10.0.0.2/24)
Test connectivity with ping from one namespace to the other’s IP address
chroot changes the apparent root directory but leaves a reference to the original root, allowing escape with sufficient privileges
pivot_root swaps the current root with a new one and moves the old root to a directory under the new root, which can then be unmounted, making escape harder

edits.title: Trap‑and‑Emulate Syscall – Detailed Ring Flow
bullets: Guest app in Ring 3 executes a software‑interrupt (e.g., INT 0x80) or privileged instruction, causing a trap that transfers control to the VMM running in Ring 0.
The CPU saves the guest’s registers in a VM‑exit structure and jumps to the VMM’s handler on its own stack.
The VMM inspects the exit, emulates the requested service, and may invoke the guest OS kernel (also in Ring 0) to perform the syscall.
The guest OS kernel processes the request, places the result in a register such as EAX, and returns control to the VMM.
The VMM restores the saved guest registers, switches back to the guest’s Ring 3 stack, and resumes the application with the result.

edits.title: Worked Example – PUSHF in Ring 3
bullets: Guest code in Ring 3 executes PUSHF, which pushes the current EFLAGS value onto the stack.
PUSHF is a sensitive‑but‑unprivileged instruction, so the CPU does not trap when it runs in Ring 3.
PUSHF pushes EFLAGS, allowing the guest to read flag bits, but POPF in Ring 3 ignores privileged bits, preventing the guest from modifying them.
Because no trap occurs, the VMM must emulate or binary‑translate PUSHF/POPF to detect and control changes to sensitive flags.
Emulation lets the VMM supply a safe EFLAGS value and preserve the equivalence property for the guest.
addresses_questions: Why was the x86 pushf/popf instruction a problem for virtualization?

edits.title: Namespace creation, unshare, and clone details
bullets: Create a new mount namespace with `unshare --mount`, separating the caller’s mount view from the parent’s view.
Before unshare, processes share a single mount tree; after unshare, the caller sees a private copy of mount points.
`clone --mount` (or `clone(..., CLONE_NEWNS)`) forks a child that starts in a fresh mount namespace with its own root filesystem view.
`setns <nsfd>` lets a running process join an existing namespace by opening the namespace file (e.g., `/proc/<pid>/ns/mnt`) and calling `setns`.
In a nested UTS namespace, a child can change its hostname without affecting the parent; each level maintains its own hostname string.
addresses_questions: If a nested namespace changes its hostname, does the parent namespace ever see that change?

edits.title: VETH pair and cgroup hierarchy examples
bullets: Create a veth pair: `ip link add veth0 type veth peer name veth1`.
Move one end into a namespace: `ip link set veth1 netns <ns_name>`; the other end stays in the host.
Assign IPs and bring interfaces up inside each namespace with `ip addr add …` and `ip link set up`.
Build a cgroup hierarchy: `mkdir -p /sys/fs/cgroup/memory/parent/child`; set a limit with `echo 209715200 > memory.limit_in_bytes` (200 MiB).
Processes placed in the child cgroup are limited by that cgroup’s settings, which can be stricter than the parent’s limits.

edits.title: Linux Namespaces Used by Docker
bullets: A Linux namespace is a kernel feature that gives a set of processes an isolated view of a particular system resource.

Docker leverages six namespaces: mount isolates filesystem mounts, pid isolates process IDs, net isolates network interfaces, ipc isolates interprocess communication, uts isolates hostname/domain, user isolates user and group IDs.
Using these namespaces, each container gets its own isolated process tree, network stack, filesystem view, IPC resources, hostname, and user mappings, providing VM‑like isolation with low overhead.
This isolation lets containers run side‑by‑side on the same host without interfering with each other's resources.

edits.title: Concrete Automation & CD Principles Rationale
bullets: Use IaC tools such as Terraform or CloudFormation to provision environments, networks, and databases automatically, removing manual setup steps.
Integrate secret‑management (e.g., HashiCorp Vault) and container image scanning (e.g., Trivy) into pipelines to replace manual credential updates and security checks.
Treat every build as a releasable artifact so you can roll back instantly, obtain rapid feedback, and keep release anxiety low because production can be updated automatically.
Trusted automated tests show a stable high pass rate, minimal flakiness, adequate code‑coverage thresholds, and run in deterministic containers that mirror production.

edits.title: Comparing Container Orchestration Tools
bullets: Docker Swarm offers simple setup with native Docker CLI, limited scalability, and built‑in overlay networking, making it suitable for small clusters or development.
Kubernetes has a steeper learning curve but provides high extensibility, can scale to thousands of nodes, uses a pluggable CNI networking model, and fits complex production workloads.
Amazon ECS integrates tightly with AWS services, leverages AWS IAM for permissions, scales within EC2 or Fargate, and is easier on AWS though less flexible than Kubernetes.
Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) delivers fully managed Kubernetes on GCP, with automatic upgrades, node provisioning, and deep integration with Google Cloud services.
Select a tool based on required scalability, cloud‑provider lock‑in, operational expertise, and need for extensibility versus simplicity.

edits.title: cgroup hierarchy example
bullets: Create a parent cgroup /myapp and two child cgroups /myapp/web and /myapp/db under the cpu and memory controllers.
Set the parent CPU quota to 100000 µs (100 % of a CPU) and memory limit to 1 GB by writing to the appropriate cgroup files.
Set child /myapp/web CPU quota to 50000 µs and memory limit to 200 MB, and set /myapp/db CPU quota to 30000 µs and memory limit to 300 MB.
Run a process in /myapp/web (e.g., cgexec -g cpu,memory:/myapp/web myserver); it cannot exceed the child limits, and the parent limits act as an overall cap.
A forked child inherits its parent’s cgroup, so it automatically follows the same CPU and memory restrictions defined for that hierarchy.

edits.title: Runtime Composition of Image Layers
bullets: Docker uses a Union File System to present all image layers as a single filesystem to the container.
Each image layer is mounted read‑only and stacked in the order they were created.
When a container starts, Docker adds a thin writable layer on top of the stack.
File reads are served from the highest layer containing the file, giving a merged view.
On write, Docker copies the file from the lower read‑only layer into the writable layer (copy‑on‑write).
addresses_questions: How do image layers work in Docker?

edits.title: Historical Conflict Between Development and Operations
bullets: Developers aim to deliver new features quickly, measuring success by release frequency and lead time.
Operations aim to keep services stable and cost‑effective, measuring success by uptime, incident rate, and resource utilization.
These differing metrics created incentives for developers to push changes rapidly while operations preferred cautious, well‑tested releases, leading to friction before DevOps.
addresses_questions: Why do development and operations teams historically have conflicting goals?
